items.title: Dysfunctional family patterns linked to adolescent depressive symptoms
items.summary:
Adolescents who experience emotional abuse face an elevated risk of developing depressive symptoms, and disruptive family dynamics appear to act as a bridge connecting these experiences. A new study tracks teenagers over a year to map how verbal hostility and manipulation at home relate to later mental health challenges, with the research published in the Journal of Clinical Psychology .

Adolescence represents a sensitive period of rapid social, cognitive, and emotional development. Teenagers undergo increased emotional reactivity and changing social relationships while consolidating their core personality traits. A supportive home environment helps build resilience, identity formation, and healthy coping strategies. Conversely, a lack of emotional validation from caregivers leaves adolescents highly vulnerable to psychological distress.

Physical abuse often leaves visible marks, but emotional abuse operates subtly and without obvious external signs. Emotional maltreatment involves behaviors like persistent criticism, verbal attacks, humiliation, manipulation, or actively withholding emotional support. Over time, these hostile interactions are associated with shame, anxiety, and chronic feelings of helplessness in youth. Such abuse can erode a teenager’s self-esteem and reduce their overall sense of emotional security.

Family functioning serves as another central component of a teenager’s psychological environment. This concept refers to the patterns family members use to communicate, manage conflict, interact, and meet each other’s emotional and practical needs.…
items.t: Dysfunctional family patterns linked to adolescent depressive symptoms

items.title: More REM sleep is linked to lower risk of dozens of diseases, wearable data from 95,000 adults suggest
items.summary:
The amount and type of sleep people get may be linked to their risk of developing a wide range of diseases, according to an analysis of data from more than 95,000 adults published in PLOS Medicine . The researchers identified 156 significant associations between sleep characteristics, measured with wrist-worn devices, and later diagnoses across more than 1,000 health conditions.

Sleep plays an essential role in maintaining physical and mental health, supporting processes such as memory, emotional regulation, and immune functioning. Previous research has linked insufficient or poor-quality sleep to conditions including cardiovascular disease and depression. However, many studies have relied on people reporting their own sleeping habits, which may not accurately reflect how much or how well they sleep.

Sleep also involves more than simply spending enough hours in bed. Throughout the night, the brain cycles through different stages, including light sleep, deep sleep, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. REM sleep is associated with vivid dreaming and processes involved in memory and emotional functioning, while deep sleep supports important restorative processes.

Although previous studies have investigated the health consequences of sleep duration, less is known about how different sleep stages, irregular sleeping patterns, and time spent awake during the night relate to the development of diseases. The researchers therefore sought to examine these relationships using movement data collected from wearable devices rather than relying solely on self-reported sleep…
items.t: More REM sleep is linked to lower risk of dozens of diseases, wearable data from 95,000 adults suggest

items.title: Your scrambled eggs aren’t just breakfast — scientists found eating at least five a week is linked to a 27 percent lower Alzheimer’s risk
items.summary:
If you’ve ever stood in front of an open fridge wondering what actually matters for keeping your mind sharp as you get older, it’s easy to assume the answer has to be complicated. A strict eating plan, maybe, or cutting out half the grocery store.

Rarely does anyone point at the carton of eggs sitting right on the shelf. Yet a large new analysis suggests this ordinary breakfast staple — whether you scramble it on a Sunday morning or eat it without thinking inside baked goods — tracks with a noticeably lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease later in life.

Even more surprising? You didn’t have to be a daily egg-eater to show up on the right side of the data.

Why skipping eggs stood out most 
 When people hear about a food linked to brain aging, the first question is usually how much of it you have to eat for it to count. In this case, the real twist wasn’t only at the top of the chart — it was at zero.

To see how everyday eating habits line up with formal diagnoses, epidemiologist Jisoo Oh, principal investigator Joan Sabaté, and their colleagues at Loma Linda University School of Public Health looked at dietary surveys from nearly 40,000 older adults in the United States and matched them to Medicare records over more than a decade and a half. Their findings appeared in The Journal of Nutrition. 

People who ate at least five eggs a week had up to a 27 percent lower risk of developing Alzheimer’s compared to those who rarely or never ate them. Yet even folks who had eggs just one to three times a month saw a 17 percent lower risk.

Meanwhile, avoiding eggs altogether stood…
items.t: Your scrambled eggs aren’t just breakfast — scientists found eating at least five a week is linked to a 27 percent lower Alzheimer’s risk

items.title: Sociologists found strict atheists aren’t the ones pairing science with ghosts and jinxes—that link appears in people straddling two worlds you’d expect to clash
items.summary:
If you’ve ever felt a twinge of unease touring a house with a grim past—or caught yourself quietly dodging a jinx even though you consider yourself a rational, science-minded person—you’re in familiar territory. Most of us assume that trusting science and brushing off official church rules gradually dries up superstition.

Actually, the pattern runs the other way, and it doesn’t belong to the group you might expect. Strict atheists aren’t the ones pairing a scientific worldview with ghosts, curses, and minor rituals. Instead, that combination turns up most strongly in people straddling two worlds—relying on science over religious doctrine while still keeping one foot in faith, whether that means believing in God, claiming a religious affiliation, or attending church services.

When science replaces church rules, not wonder 
 We tend to picture reason and the supernatural as a simple seesaw: when science goes up, everything eerie or mystical drops out. In everyday life, though, stepping away from institutional authority rarely flips an off switch on curiosity about unseen forces.

What fades first is the official, church-approved version of the supernatural. People who lean on science to understand the world and prefer making moral choices from human experience rather than religious teachings are much less likely to believe in traditional, God-created miracles.

Yet that same independent outlook tracks with stronger belief in everyday superstitions—like performing small rituals to ward off bad outcomes, avoiding jinxes, or feeling uncomfortable buying a home where a murder…
items.t: Sociologists found strict atheists aren’t the ones pairing science with ghosts and jinxes—that link appears in people straddling two worlds you’d expect to clash

items.title: Testing the “Love Island effect”: Midseason body pressure predicts dieting, exercise, and cosmetic desires
items.summary:
Young viewers who feel sustained pressure about their appearance while watching Love Island tend to report more weight-loss habits, muscle-building efforts, and interest in cosmetic procedures by the season’s end, according to research published in Psychology of Popular Media . Pressure felt during the opening week did not show the same link, indicating that timing may matter. The findings also suggest a partial two-way cycle, as viewers who began the season wanting cosmetic procedures tended to feel greater body pressure a month later.

Love Island is a popular British reality dating series that airs daily over eight weeks, placing young single contestants in a Spanish villa under constant video surveillance as they pair up to avoid elimination. Cast members spend much of the show in swimwear and overwhelmingly have slim, toned, and often cosmetically enhanced bodies, with many working beforehand as models, personal trainers, or social media influencers.

Those casting choices have fueled public concern about a “Love Island Effect” on young audiences. Critics worry that watching the show intensifies body pressure, meaning a felt expectation to improve or alter one’s physical appearance to match idealized standards, and encourages body change strategies. In this research, those strategies included active behaviors like changing eating habits to lose weight or exercising to build muscle, alongside wanting cosmetic procedures such as Botox, lip fillers, liposuction, or breast augmentation.

Whether idealized bodies in media actually harm viewers’ body image has been a…

items.title: How narcissistic employees manipulate their way to the top
items.summary:
Employees with narcissistic traits actively try to shrink the gap between themselves and their bosses by bonding, asking for favors, and gossiping about coworkers. These individuals hold an inflated belief that their managers prefer them over their peers, which emboldens their manipulative workplace tactics. The research was published in the Journal of Organizational Behavior .

Psychologists describe grandiose narcissism as a personality trait involving highly inflated self-views, a strong need for status, and a persistent drive to prove one’s superiority. People with these traits often pose challenges in professional environments. They tend to engage in counterproductive behaviors and can undermine the integrity of their organizations.

Past organizational research has overwhelmingly focused on narcissistic managers and executives. Bosses with inflated egos attract attention because they already hold high-status positions and wield power over others. But every professional starts their career in a subordinate role. Occupying a lower rank fundamentally clashes with a narcissistic person’s belief in their own superiority.

Judy Qiu, a researcher at ESSEC Business School in France, and Selin Kesebir, a researcher at London Business School, wanted to understand how these individuals manage the discomfort of taking orders. Leaders control access to resources, high-profile projects, and promotions. The researchers suspected that narcissistic employees would direct their interpersonal maneuvering upward to secure these benefits and gain status.

Psychological theory suggests…
items.t: How narcissistic employees manipulate their way to the top

items.title: Even mild ADHD symptoms in adolescence are linked to later antisocial and criminal behavior, twin study finds
items.summary:
An analysis of data from a long-running Finnish twin study found that adolescents with more ADHD symptoms, even at levels below the threshold for a diagnosis, tended to report more antisocial behavior and criminal activity in adulthood. These associations did not depend on participants’ cognitive abilities, and comparisons between twins suggested they were not fully explained by family background. The paper was published in Development and Psychopathology .

People with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) often experience difficulties with attention, impulse control, and regulating their behavior. Research has shown that individuals with ADHD are more likely to engage in antisocial behavior and criminal activities, with this increased risk extending even to those whose ADHD symptoms are not severe enough to warrant a clinical diagnosis. However, not everyone with ADHD symptoms develops antisocial tendencies, raising questions about what makes some individuals more vulnerable than others.

One possibility is that ADHD symptoms and antisocial behavior share genetic and environmental risk factors, rather than ADHD symptoms directly contributing to antisocial behavior. Another possibility is that certain individual characteristics protect people with ADHD symptoms from developing antisocial tendencies. Intelligence may be one such protective factor, as previous research has linked higher cognitive ability to a lower risk of criminal offending, particularly among individuals already at increased risk. Executive functions, including planning, working memory, impulse…
items.t: Even mild ADHD symptoms in adolescence are linked to later antisocial and criminal behavior, twin study finds

items.title: Psilocybin-assisted therapy linked to reduced drinking and higher odds of abstinence
items.summary:
Psilocybin-assisted therapy appears to offer moderate short-term reductions in drinking and improved odds of remaining abstinent over several months for people with alcohol use disorder, according to a systematic review and meta-analysis published in Journal of Psychopharmacology . Pooling data from six modern clinical trials, the researchers found that the medically supervised treatment was generally well tolerated, with mostly mild and short-lived side effects. Although longer-term advantages varied across drinking measures, the findings suggest the approach could eventually become a viable addition to existing addiction care.

Alcohol use disorder is a chronic medical condition marked by a persistent inability to cut back or stop drinking alcohol despite serious harm to a person’s health, relationships, or daily responsibilities. Standard care includes prescription medications such as naltrexone or acamprosate, which target brain pathways involved in cravings and reward, alongside talk therapies like cognitive behavioral therapy and motivational interviewing. Even after receiving these established treatments, many patients return to heavy drinking, driving clinical interest in new therapeutic options.

One emerging option is psilocybin-assisted therapy, in which a patient takes one or more medically supervised doses of psilocybin, the active psychedelic compound in certain mushrooms. Clinics pair those dosing sessions with preparatory counseling beforehand and integration sessions afterward to help patients process the experience. Earlier brain imaging research in…
items.t: Psilocybin-assisted therapy linked to reduced drinking and higher odds of abstinence

items.title: People with borderline personality disorder are more likely to mistake accidental harm for deliberate harm, study finds
items.summary:
People with borderline personality disorder are more likely than healthy adults to misread accidental harm as deliberate, according to new research published in Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging . They recognized genuinely intentional harm just as accurately, so the difficulty appears specific to ambiguous situations rather than a blanket assumption of hostile intent. Brain-wave recordings also showed them drawing the line between accident and intent later than healthy adults did.

Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a mental health condition marked by intense emotional swings, impulsive behavior, and unstable interpersonal relationships, affecting an estimated 1.2% to 6% of the general population. Beyond difficulties with mood and impulse control, the condition frequently involves challenges in social cognition, the mental processes people rely on to interpret what others are thinking and feeling. In particular, the authors of a 2013 review noted that clinical research consistently points to negative biases in how people with the condition judge others, including a tendency to suspect malevolent motives.

Supporting that broader picture, a 2021 meta-analysis of 34 studies involving more than 3,400 participants found that people with borderline personality disorder showed modest difficulty reasoning about others’ mental states alongside a stronger tendency to overinterpret other people’s intentions. Challenges with ambiguous cues also appear in everyday speech, with a behavioral study of adults with borderline personality disorder finding…
items.t: People with borderline personality disorder are more likely to mistake accidental harm for deliberate harm, study finds

items.title: Psychology says people who struggle with a low sex drive are bothered most by one fear
items.summary:
If you’ve ever lain awake wondering why your sex drive seems to have vanished for weeks, you know how quickly that silence can turn into self-doubt. You start running a quiet audit in your head. Is something off? Shouldn’t you want this more often?

What tends to sting most in those moments isn’t only missing the spark you used to feel. Often, the heaviest part is a quieter fear aimed at someone else: the nagging worry that you aren’t satisfying your partner.

It feels like a solitary problem, partly because few people bring it up over coffee. Yet that private unease turns out to be remarkably common — and it rarely stays neatly inside the bedroom. Everyday mental health, deep exhaustion, and the quiet pressures of partnership sit right behind how people judge their own desire.

Why the worry lands on your relationship 
 That picture comes into focus in research published in the Journal of Sex & Marital Therapy by Caroline F. Pukall, a psychology professor at Queen’s University in Kingston, Ontario, and her colleagues. To move past purely clinical cases and see how ordinary people experience desire day to day, the team ran an online survey combining multiple-choice questions with open-ended prompts where respondents could explain their thoughts in their own words.

Across the adult respondents, 57.1 percent said they had worried about their sex drive. Most feared their desire was too low, and among the worried group, 42.4 percent pointed to a mismatch between their own appetite and their partner’s.

When people dealing with low desire were asked what troubled them most,…
items.t: Psychology says people who struggle with a low sex drive are bothered most by one fear

items.title: Marking an informational text as AI-generated does not influence its ratings, study finds
items.summary:
An online experiment conducted in Germany found that labeling a short nutrition text as written by artificial intelligence did not meaningfully change how participants rated it. However, many participants did not notice the label: only about 42% of those who read the AI-labeled text reported that a source had been mentioned. The paper was published in Applied Psychology: Health and Well-Being .

Since the release of ChatGPT in 2022, artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots have become increasingly popular, with growing numbers of people using them for everyday tasks and information seeking. Although most users turn to AI for writing, education, and general inquiries, a smaller but growing proportion seek health-related information and advice.

AI chatbots have the potential to improve public health communication by providing accessible explanations of scientific findings, summarizing medical guidelines, and correcting misinformation. However, research suggests that AI-generated health and nutrition advice is not always accurate, raising questions about whether people should trust and follow such recommendations. Previous studies have produced inconsistent findings, with some reporting lower trust in AI-generated advice and others finding that people evaluate AI-generated information as favorably as human-generated content.

Study author Laura M. König and colleagues wanted to find out whether informational texts labeled as AI-generated are rated differently from texts with no source information, and whether prior experience with AI changes this. They also examined which…
items.t: Marking an informational text as AI-generated does not influence its ratings, study finds

items.title: Reminiscing about an ex isn’t always bad for your love life — a psychology experiment found it left dating adults happier with their partner
items.summary:
If you’ve ever caught yourself smiling at a sudden memory of an ex while sitting next to someone you genuinely like, you probably know the quiet guilt that follows. Most of us assume sentimental memories have a strict loyalty rule: warm flashbacks about your current partner are healthy, while fond thoughts of an old flame mean something is off.

We tend to sort romantic nostalgia into neat categories of safe and risky. One is supposed to bring you closer to the person you’re with; the other is supposed to quietly pull you away.

Yet romantic memory rarely cooperates with that tidy script. Thinking warmly about a past love doesn’t always undermine the relationship you’re in — and looking back on sweet moments with your current partner can turn out to be far more bittersweet than people expect.

When remembering your current partner feels bittersweet 
 In a study published in Emotion, psychologist Soo Yeon Park, now at the University of Florida, and her colleagues tested what actually happens when people lean into nostalgic memories of love past versus love present.

They split 172 unmarried dating adults in Korea — all with at least one prior committed relationship — into three groups: one wrote about a nostalgic memory of an ex, another wrote about a nostalgic moment with their current partner, and a third simply described their previous week. Before and after writing, everyone rated their relationship happiness and commitment, then reported the emotions the task brought up.

Contrary to what Park’s team expected, looking back on an ex didn’t drag down people’s present…
items.t: Reminiscing about an ex isn’t always bad for your love life — a psychology experiment found it left dating adults happier with their partner

items.title: A child’s early test scores aren’t just an academic milestone — psychology researchers discovered they are linked to how their mother’s physical health holds up
items.summary:
Sitting at a kitchen table, patiently running through spelling words or math flashcards with your child, is a familiar milestone. In those moments, you are almost certainly thinking about how that hard work will shape their future. You hope a solid grip on math and reading will help them do well in school, get a good job, and navigate life. But there is a quiet, surprising possibility: those kitchen-table study sessions might also track your own well-being decades down the road.

Mothers often worry that their health problems might weigh on their children. However, new research suggests that this generational highway might actually run both ways. How easily a child learns could have a surprisingly close tie to how their mother fares, physically and mentally, as she gets older.

A surprisingly close connection 
 A study published in the journal Intelligence explored this cross-generational link by diving into data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth, a long-running US project that tracked more than 11,000 children and their mothers over several decades.

Led by researcher Linda Wänström and her colleagues, the team analyzed reading and math assessment scores taken by children between the ages of 5 and 15, alongside health data gathered from their mothers as they reached their 40s and 50s. At those milestone ages, the mothers self-reported on their physical health, mental well-being, and depression symptoms.

When the researchers looked at the family as a unit, they discovered something remarkable. Mothers whose children scored higher on math and reading tests…
items.t: A child’s early test scores aren’t just an academic milestone — psychology researchers discovered they are linked to how their mother’s physical health holds up

items.title: Smartphone ownership at age 12 linked to higher risk of eating disorder symptoms two years later
items.summary:
Owning a personal smartphone by age 12 is associated with a higher likelihood of experiencing eating disorder symptoms both at that age and two years later, according to a large national study published in JAMA Network Open . Analyzing data from nearly 9,000 U.S. adolescents, researchers found that early smartphone owners were more likely to report symptoms such as binge eating, unhealthy attempts to prevent weight gain, and basing their self-worth on their body weight. The findings suggest that the timing of a child’s first smartphone may be tied to eating disorder risk during a sensitive stage of adolescent development.

Eating disorders are serious mental health conditions marked by persistent disruptions in eating habits along with distressing thoughts or behaviors centered on food, body weight, or physical shape. In the United States, eating disorders that meet full clinical criteria are estimated to affect 3.4% to 3.8% of adolescent girls and 1.2% to 1.5% of adolescent boys, while disordered eating behaviors that fall short of a formal diagnosis are much more widespread.

A systematic review of data from 16 countries estimated that slightly more than one in five adolescents engage in some form of disordered eating. Even milder symptoms can interfere with daily functioning and raise the likelihood of more severe problems over time.

Early adolescence, spanning roughly ages 10 to 14, is a developmental window when young people seek greater independence and peer approval while brain systems for self-regulation are still maturing. Puberty also brings rapid bodily changes…
items.t: Smartphone ownership at age 12 linked to higher risk of eating disorder symptoms two years later

How do I navigate being single when I’m not interested in sex with near strangers? I don’t judge anyone, consenting adults can do whatever they like – but, for me, sex has to come with trust and, frankly, love, or at least the potential of love. I’m recently single after a long and toxic relationship, and I’ve never dated – I got on the dating scene and found that if I don’t try to get in someone’s pants by the third date, no matter how much of a nice time we’re having, they disappear – and in fact I’ve had some women do the old “call yourself a man” at me, in one memorable case, after they specifically said “not tonight” and I said “no problem” (the response was a frustrated “don’t you have needs?!”).

I’ve tried to go along with it and do what’s expected but I don’t enjoy it, it just feels a bit wrong, and when I’ve done this it kills the vibe we had, probably because I can’t get into it properly. I’ve always been into the person, not just the body, but it takes time to get to know someone enough to feel comfortable being intimate. So how can I keep a nice relationship going, so that I can develop the trust I need for sex, without them losing interest because I’m not doing (what I assume) everyone else on the dating scene is…

items.title: Happiness appears to lead to a sense of purpose, but not the other way around, according to new psychology research
items.summary:
People often assume that finding a mission in life leads to greater happiness, but new research suggests the opposite sequence might be more accurate. A study published in The Journal of Positive Psychology found that experiencing happiness predicts the later development of a sense of purpose, while having a purpose does not predict future happiness. The results indicate that feeling good may provide the emotional foundation necessary to pursue meaningful, long-term life goals.

Happiness and purpose are distinct but related aspects of human well-being. Psychologists generally define happiness as a global, subjective evaluation of one’s life. It involves experiencing frequent positive emotions, infrequent negative emotions, and a general sense that life is highly satisfying. Rather than simply adding up pleasant moments, a happy person intuits that their life as a whole is going well.

Purpose involves setting and pursuing long-term goals that organize a person’s behavior. A person with a strong sense of purpose holds overarching aims that dictate how they spend their time, energy, and resources. While purpose does not strictly require an individual to be happy, people who report having a life mission often report high levels of life satisfaction.

Researchers have frequently studied these two dimensions of well-being, but they usually do so by looking at people at a single point in time. This approach makes it difficult to tell if one psychological state precedes the other. The temporal sequence between the two states has remained an open question.

items.t: Happiness appears to lead to a sense of purpose, but not the other way around, according to new psychology research

items.title: People with depression who use psilocybin are not abandoning standard mental health care, study suggests
items.summary:
People with depression who use psilocybin mushrooms do not appear to be abandoning standard psychiatric care, according to a new nationally representative study published in Psychological Medicine . Instead, they use conventional services such as outpatient care, telehealth, and prescription medications at roughly the same rates as depressed individuals who do not use psilocybin, while being notably more likely to feel their mental health care needs are going unmet. The findings suggest that real-world psilocybin use among people with depression often coexists with ongoing struggles to obtain adequate relief or care.

Psilocybin is a naturally occurring psychedelic compound found in certain species of mushrooms that alters mood, perception, and thinking by interacting with serotonin pathways in the brain. Public interest in the substance has grown alongside state and local policy changes, including decriminalization in several U.S. jurisdictions, and clinical trials showing that psilocybin-assisted therapy can reduce symptoms of major depression. An observational analysis tracking U.S. trends between 2019 and 2023 found that psilocybin use climbed sharply across age groups during that period, with particularly high rates among people experiencing moderate to severe symptoms of depression or anxiety.

In clinical trials, psilocybin is administered under tightly controlled conditions that include measured dosing, trained psychological support, and medical supervision. Outside of research settings, however, people take mushrooms in unstructured environments ranging from music…
items.t: People with depression who use psilocybin are not abandoning standard mental health care, study suggests

items.title: Psychology says frequent worry isn’t a sure sign of shorter nights — it tracks with reporting less sleep, but not what wrist monitors recorded
items.summary:
There’s a particular kind of guesswork that kicks in whenever someone asks how many hours you usually sleep. You don’t pull out a spreadsheet — you go by feel, running a quick mental tally of late nights, groggy mornings, and every stretch you remember staring at the ceiling.

For people who naturally lean toward worry, that mental tally often comes up short. It feels obvious enough: a busy, uneasy mind ought to steal hours from your night.

Yet how much sleep you feel like you’re getting and what a wrist-worn tracker logs don’t always line up. And the gap between the two may have less to do with a stressful week than with a steadier part of who you are.

When the numbers don’t match your memory 
 When you try to judge your own rest, you aren’t reading off an objective clock. You’re piecing together weeks of nights from memory — a process that can easily lean on how restful or restless those nights felt.

To see how personality relates to that estimate, researchers Derick M. DeCamp and Elizabeth J. Pantesco of Villanova University put self-reported sleep side by side with wearable data. Their study, published in Personality and Individual Differences, followed 134 undergraduate students without diagnosed sleep disorders who filled out questionnaires on personality, typical sleep, and symptoms of depression and anxiety while wearing a movement-tracking wrist device for five nights.

A clear split emerged around neuroticism, the personality trait tied to experiencing worry and negative emotions more easily. Students who scored higher on neuroticism consistently reported…
items.t: Psychology says frequent worry isn’t a sure sign of shorter nights — it tracks with reporting less sleep, but not what wrist monitors recorded

items.title: Scientists used a Harry Potter soundtrack and implanted electrodes to challenge a common assumption about how we hear
items.summary:
In a typical movie scene, spoken dialogue weaves in and out of an orchestral score, often playing at the exact same moment. A new study published in Science Advances suggests that the human auditory cortex tracks basic pitch-and-timing fluctuations in sound waves closely enough to support the perceptual distinction between speech and music on that basis alone. Using direct recordings from inside the brains of hospitalized patients, researchers reconstructed those acoustic patterns and predicted when a separate group of listeners heard speech or music, even as the two overlapped.

Human hearing relies heavily on the auditory cortex, a sheet of neural tissue in the brain’s outer layer folded along the upper ridges of the temporal lobes, just above each ear. Cells in this tissue respond to spectrotemporal modulations, which are the combined physical patterns of how a sound wave’s energy fluctuates across pitch frequencies and over time. Temporal modulations reflect how rapidly loudness rises and falls, like the brisk cadence of spoken syllables, whereas spectral modulations describe how closely spaced a sound’s pitch components are, like the notes of a musical chord.

Neuroscientists debate whether tracking these raw acoustic building blocks is enough for the auditory cortex to separate speech from music, or whether the brain relies on dedicated neural modules for abstract sound categories. Several brain-imaging studies have pointed to specialized neural groups in secondary auditory areas that respond selectively to speech, music, or song. Consistent with a mix of shared and…
items.t: Scientists used a Harry Potter soundtrack and implanted electrodes to challenge a common assumption about how we hear

items.title: Psychology says it’s not the big public shout-out that makes you feel most supported — it’s something far quieter and ordinary
items.summary:
Think about the last time someone really came through for you. Maybe a friend dropped everything to help you move, or a coworker quietly rescued a project before a deadline. 

In that moment, you have a small choice to make. You can sit with that warm feeling privately, post a glowing shout-out on social media for everyone to see, or pull out your phone and fire off a quick, direct text. 

Most of us treat that choice as an afterthought. If anything, a casual text can feel like the lowest-effort option compared with writing a heartfelt letter or honoring someone in front of an audience online. Yet when psychologists put those everyday habits head-to-head, the humble text message turned out to carry a surprising social punch. 

Why how you say thanks matters 
 For years, gratitude exercises have been one of the most popular tools in positive psychology. Classic approaches usually look like keeping a private gratitude list—noting good things like your health or a sunny morning—or writing a formal thank-you letter. 

Researchers draw a useful line between two flavors of gratitude. There is gratitude for the positive parts of your life, and there is gratitude to a specific person whose kindness made a difference. Both can lift your mood, though gratitude directed toward another person naturally pulls you into a social space. 

Even so, psychologists have pointed out that much of the older research on gratitude came from small studies that weren’t preregistered, leaving big questions about how the social side of giving thanks actually works. Does keeping appreciation to…
items.t: Psychology says it’s not the big public shout-out that makes you feel most supported — it’s something far quieter and ordinary

Deprivation is behind the sharp rise highlighted in the Natsal study, and that’s an outrage. High energy bills should never be a factor in reproductive choice

The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal) is the crowdpleaser of the data world. Nerds love it because of its extraordinary thoroughness. It’s one of the largest studies of sexual behaviour in the world, surveying nearly 7,000 people in the UK between the ages of 16 and 59, once a decade. Everyone else loves it because they get to talk about sex. Some of the statistics speak for themselves – among 25- to 34-year-old women, the number who say they never want children has gone up fourfold, a sad, completely understandable reflection of the outside world.

Other figures, though, are mysterious: the number of women aged 16 to 24 who are on the pill has dropped precipitously, from nearly half to less than a third. Over the same period, the online space has been flooded with information about hormonal contraception, some of it better than it has ever been – more accessible, more accurate – and some of it plain wrong. items.title: Psychology says going silent on a text isn’t proof someone doesn’t care—people who stop replying tend to feel worse than you realize
items.summary:
There’s a particular kind of quiet that settles in after you send a casual text and get nothing back. An hour passes, then an afternoon, then a couple of days, and your brain starts filling in the blank—usually in the least generous way possible.

Did you come across as annoying? Did you say something weird? Mostly, it’s easy to assume the person on the other end saw your message, shrugged, and didn’t think twice about ignoring you.

We tend to picture ghosting as a cold, deliberate brush-off. In everyday digital life, though, silence is often far messier: someone glances at a text while distracted, means to answer later, and forgets, or puts off replying without realizing the other person already feels shut out.

The quiet side of the screen 
 Research suggests that when a conversation goes dark, the person who stopped replying is rarely as unbothered as they look from the outside.

To examine how both sides misread unanswered messages, Sophia Li of the Haas School of Business at the University of California, Berkeley, and Coral Zheng of the University of Cambridge’s Judge Business School ran a series of studies published in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin. Asking adults to recall past online exchanges, imagine texting with a casual friend, and chat live with strangers, they compared how bad people actually felt about going quiet with how bad the waiting side expected them to feel.

In both the recalled and imagined conversations, people who stopped responding felt—or expected to feel—worse than those left waiting predicted. When adults looked back on real…
items.t: Psychology says going silent on a text isn’t proof someone doesn’t care—people who stop replying tend to feel worse than you realize

items.title: When Your Doctor Prescribes a Visit to an Art Gallery
items.summary:
The soulful deep greens and browns of British Columbia’s forests weave together with ferns and moss, catching the light through the tops of ancient firs and cedars. The trees sway, and the earth rises and falls among the rocks. 

But in this case, the view isn’t from the trail. It is a painting by Canadian artist Emily Carr on display in the Vancouver Art Gallery , and some of those who are experiencing it are doing so because it was prescribed by their health care provider. How they ended up there is the result of a bit of creative thinking that honors the role of art in healing.

In 2025, the gallery partnered with BC Parks Foundation to extend PaRx , Canada’s national nature prescription program, to include the gallery. PaRx is a successful initiative that has included an estimated 2 million prescriptions issued by more than 20,000 health care providers. Typically, these prescriptions are for time outdoors, with added benefits, like free transportation, to reduce barriers to access.

Using art as an entry point into nature as a formal intervention is novel—the first collaboration of its kind between a nature prescription program and an arts institution in the world, according to Sirish Rao, the gallery’s co-CEO and executive director. While art-based prescriptions are gaining in popularity, this program goes a step further, integrating engagement with nature in a gentle, accessible way. Other institutions around the world are looking to the Vancouver Art Gallery program as a model initiative that can be replicated in other communities to support people’s well-being.…
items.t: When Your Doctor Prescribes a Visit to an Art Gallery

items.title: What Happens When Elders Share Their Stories
items.summary:
When I moved from the San Francisco Bay Area to a small, rural town in Vermont, I wanted to find a way to contribute to the local community. Knowing there was a significant senior population here, I reached out to the town librarian with hopes of helping elders share their stories. 

The local historical society took interest in this idea, which led to an exhibit at the 159-year-old Tunbridge World’s Fair, and a book series entitled Folk Life: Tunbridge Oral Histories . The first two print runs sold out. The second collection of stories has just been published, and people are already asking who will be featured in the third. 

What is it about life stories that strikes such a universal chord? And why is it important—and even imperative—to share our stories with others? I interviewed oral historians, teachers, and a digital storyteller to discover more about why the age-old tradition of recording oral histories continues to make such a significant impact for individuals and communities.

Fostering connections and reflection 

Storytelling is, according to scientific research, a biological shortcut to human connection. Uri Hasson and fellow researchers at Princeton University discovered that the brains of the storyteller and listener physically sync up while a story is being told, promoting social connection, trust, and empathy. 

The more emotionally affecting the story is, the stronger this connection becomes. As emotions and tension rise, hormones are released, including oxytocin, the “bonding hormone”; dopamine, which sharpens focus; and cortisol, which promotes…
items.t: What Happens When Elders Share Their Stories
